message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name

A few for the staff vote:
- **Chester Drawers**
- **Vincent Van Go**
- **Vantique**
- **Sofa So Good**
- **The Dovetail**

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

**This is the only order that works.**
- **C has to come last,** because it won't accept anything before 11:00, while A and B both need delivering before 10:00.
- **B has to come before A.** If he does A first, he arrives at A at 09:00, finishes at 09:15, and reaches B at 09:40, which is after B opens at 09:30.

| Time | Activity | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot | Not before 08:30 ✓ |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B, unload | |
| 09:05 | Finish at B, leave for A | Done before 09:30 ✓ (25 min spare) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A, unload | |
| 09:45 | Finish at A, leave for C | Within 09:00–10:00 ✓ (15 min spare) |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C | Too early for C |
| **10:25–10:55** | **30-minute break** | Fits in the wait ✓ |
| 11:00 | Unload at C | Not before 11:00 ✓ |
| 11:15 | Leave C | |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** | **Exactly on the limit** |

**The return has no slack at all.** Starting at C at 11:00, unloading for 15 minutes and driving 45 minutes back gives 12:00 whatever order the earlier drops are in. Any delay at C, such as waiting for someone to sign or a slow unload, makes the van late.

I've also assumed the drive from C back to the depot takes the same 45 minutes as the drive out, since you didn't give that time.

To build in a margin:
- ask the office at C whether 10:45 would be acceptable, which buys 15 minutes; or
- call ahead so someone is ready to receive at exactly 11:00; or
- check whether "back by 12:00" has any give.

Also check that someone will be at shop B to receive the delivery at 08:50, before it opens.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] is on its way and should arrive in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **No new damage.** Check for scratches, dents or marks on the finish, comparing against photos taken when it was loaded.
2. **Everything is there.** That includes handles, keys, shelves, legs, glass and any loose parts.
3. **It works and stands properly.** Drawers and doors open smoothly, and it sits level without rocking.

Ask the customer to look it over with the driver before signing.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, signed on a phone or tablet at the door.** It's harder to lose, you keep a searchable record, and you can attach photos of the item at handover. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who don't use email.

## Proof of delivery, in a line

> **Proof of delivery is a record, usually a signature, photo and time, showing that the customer received their item and in what condition.**

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], [Business] here. Your furniture is due tomorrow 9-10am. We'll text when the driver's on the way. Any problems, just reply. Thanks!

With a five-letter name and a 20-character business name, this comes to about **150 characters**. Longer names push it up, so keep the business name short, or drop "Thanks!" if needed.

Use **straight apostrophes** ('), not curly ones ('), and no emoji. A single curly apostrophe or emoji can switch the text to a format with a 70-character limit, which would split it into several messages.
